projectTitle: Enzymatic degradation of wind turbine blade epoxy
tagline: A chemo-enzymatic route to the resin fraction of decommissioned wind turbine blades, assessed honestly against the alternatives
summary: DTU engineered laccases (ItL-03 from a spruce bark beetle gut metagenome, CueO variants and homologues) and unspecific peroxygenases (PaDa-I, WamPa, PabUPO-II, MroUPO, Fett) to attack the amine crosslinks of cured epoxy from wind turbine blades, layered on top of a published acid-plus-peroxide solvolysis pretreatment. They used NNBT, a small water-soluble molecule carrying the tertiary amine of the crosslink, as a defined model substrate, and showed by MALDI-TOF that PaDa-I performs N-dealkylation on it with Purpald confirmation of lactaldehyde release. The decisive work is a prospective comparative life-cycle assessment in SimaPro (ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint H) of five end-of-life routes, which found their own enzymatic route is NOT the best option on almost any indicator - and they published that. Seven interviews across DTU Wind, DTU Sustain, DTU Chemistry, SDU and industry, plus documented non-responses from Siemens Gamesa, Orsted and MAKEEN Energy, drove changes to the chemical target, the model substrate, the host organism, the enzyme-ranking criterion and the project's stated goal.

dry.frameworks: Three parallel enzyme-discovery pipelines agreed after advice from the 2025 team's dry-lab head: an 'easy' track of literature enzymes known to oxidise the relevant bonds, a 'medium' track of homologue mining, and a 'hard' track of rational engineering and generative design. Plus a prospective comparative LCA (SimaPro, ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint H, functional unit of blade mass with cutting/transport/metal separation excluded as identical across routes) and a Kremser-equation model of the countercurrent solvent extraction stage.
dry.dataviz: An interactive clickable process-flow diagram that zooms from the five-route overview into the enzymatic routes with every parameter on the box (acid molarity, temperature, residence time, enzyme loading in mg/L, number of reuses, recovery fractions); one SDG per plot with burdens above zero and credits below; an interactive stakeholder map where each pin opens the interview, colour-coded by engagement status so non-responses stay visible.
dry.datascience: Sequence mining of UniProt, Pfam and BLAST rather than metagenomic libraries; multiple sequence alignment to transfer organic-solvent-tolerance mutations from PaDa-I onto GroGu and PabUPO-II; a novel substrate-access-channel discovery pipeline used in place of docking affinity ranking; molecular dynamics; generative enzyme design on the DTU HPC. Every LCA parameter is published with its source, the mismatch between source and use, and a 'weakest link' label (e.g. partition coefficients taken from a 1980 phenol-extraction paper using MIBK rather than ethyl acetate, flagged explicitly).
dry.software: LCA input data, assumptions and mapping code released open source so other teams can rebuild the model in SimaPro or another tool; lectures, workshops and guides collected on the contribution page.
techniques: CO-difference spectroscopy for correctly folded heme

good.publicEngagement: Education was pointed at the specific blind spot the project exposed rather than at synthetic biology in general: visits to international high schools taught the wind sector's end-of-life emissions and the idea of thinking in full sustainability circles early, and a Lifelong Learning workshop took the same low-impact recycling discussion to an audience of working professionals. For the iGEM community they ran a BioBrick workshop, an intellectual-property introduction ('Protecting Your Ideas'), a World Cafe team-to-team roundtable and a podcast, and presented at the Nordic iGEM Conference. State of Green gave them a platform to put the blade-waste problem to people from ministries, academia and the energy sector.
good.ihp: DTU's IHP is built as a decision trail, not a visitor log: every interview card carries an explicit 'Implementation' list, and there is a separate section on approaches they chose NOT to pursue. The single biggest change came from Dr Javier (Postdoc, DTU Sustain, one of the few in his group working on resin chemistry rather than glass-fibre recovery) across two interviews on 3 March and 24 June 2026. He posed what the team calls the sharpest experimental question raised in the project - can an enzyme replace the cleaving solvent, acting on a swollen but still crosslinked network? - and told them to start from a well-documented literature pretreatment rather than invent one and layer enzymes on top. The result was a hard reframing: the enzymatic step stopped being a standalone degradation claim and became a complement to solvolysis, with a new explicit objective of testing whether enzymes could substitute for part of the solvent-cleavage step, and a second research line on engineering solvent tolerance into the enzymes. Justine Beauson (Senior Researcher, Composites Manufacturing and Testing, DTU Wind) was the first contact; she confirmed thermoset epoxy is what is coming down now, referred the team to a turbine OEM, and in a 6 October email follow-up explained that the Blade Material Passport is compiled independently of any thinking about disposal and will tell you a blade is epoxy but never the formulation - which is why the team abandoned any attempt to match real blade resin and why 'collaboration between the production and the waste-management industries' became the organising claim on the sustainability page. Jesper Kjaer Jorgensen (Postdoc, Composites, DTU) then supplied fully cured SWANCOR 2519-1A/BS, a commercial non-NDA amine-cured bisphenol-A epoxy, and agreed with the team's hypothesis that the tertiary amine crosslink is the vulnerable point: the team writes plainly that 'without those cubes we would have had either no workable material or a different one', and the target shifted from the epoxy backbone to the amine crosslinks, changing which bonds they went after, how they measured degradation and which products they hoped to recover. Robert (PhD, Eukaryotic Molecular Cell Biology) delivered the hardest reality check - thermoset degradation is heavily researched, the field contains many low-quality papers with missing controls and uncharacterised substrates, and a six-month student project cannot run a metagenomic discovery campaign - and the team's response is laid out item by item: they screened roughly 33 enzymes rather than thousands, worked from public databases rather than metagenomic libraries, used a colorimetric assay rather than a fluorescent reporter, added MALDI-TOF, and had a postdoc rather than students perform the hazardous epoxy pretreatment. Carlos G. Acevedo-Rocha (Senior Researcher, Computational Protein Engineering, BRIGHT) told them not to base findings on docking affinity values because there is no significant correlation with experimental activity, and endorsed their early-stage channel-discovery pipeline: they abandoned the plan to filter homologue candidates on Boltz-2 affinity scores and rebuilt candidate selection around channel geometry plus molecular dynamics. Cecilia Castellvi Domingo (PhD, heterologous expression of UPOs) changed the chassis and the protocol - Komagataella phaffii on an episomal AP17 backbone rather than S. cerevisiae or E. coli, harvest at day 5 instead of day 6 to reduce proteolysis, lower induction temperature, and the CO-difference spectrum assay that gave them a direct measurement of correctly folded heme-containing enzyme (0.019 uM in a six-fold concentrated sample) that activity assays could not. Lykke Margot Ricard (Associate Professor in Sustainable Innovation, SDU, who had mapped Danish blade treatment options for the Danish EPA) asked who the retaker is, and in response every workstream was required to name a recoverable product, the quality it would need and a potential buyer - which is also why the team says the ideal process recovers a product rather than incinerating residues. The European Environment Agency answered that it holds no data on retired blade management, that the WEEE Directive does not cover wind turbines and that no dedicated EU legislation exists, so there is no reporting obligation; the team then marked the landfill share as an unverifiable input in the LCA rather than quoting a number. Most unusually, they publish their failures of access: Siemens Gamesa never replied to email and had no relevant expert at the DSE careers fair, nobody at Orsted could speak to blade end-of-life, MAKEEN Energy did not reply, and the team states outright that the groups with the greatest influence over adoption 'were therefore among the least represented in our discussions, limiting our analysis' - and makes those gaps visible on the stakeholder map, which rates each group by influence over adoption and interest separately, including 'unknown' for potential buyers of recovered compounds because no market has been shown to exist.
good.realWorld: The need is a quantified bottleneck rather than a slogan: Danish blade waste currently goes to mixed-waste landfill or is shipped abroad by lorry and ferry, the Danish wind industry's voluntary landfill ban took effect on 1 January 2026, a Danish EPA screening detected bisphenol A in every tank leaching test on blade material, and the EEA confirmed there is no EU legislation or reporting obligation for wind-turbine waste at all pending the WEEE revision in the Circular Economy Act. SDGs are justified target by target with numbers from their own LCA, and the headline finding is one most teams would hide: in the base industrial scale-up scenario (projected to about 2035) the enzymatic route emits 2.1 kg CO2 eq per kg of blade against 1.4 for solvolysis and 0.9 for pyrolysis, adds 0.38 person-equivalents of human carcinogenic toxicity against 0.022 for solvolysis, uses about 36% more water, and cement co-processing is best on almost every indicator - so they state that enzymatic and solvolysis are the only routes with clear net burdens, trace the hotspot to the H2O2 supply chain and UPO production, and convert that into a research direction (make UPO production more efficient, recover a product instead of incinerating residues, reuse immobilised enzyme and compute the break-even number of reuses). SDG targets are matched one-to-one with their own data on SDG 3 (illness from hazardous chemicals), 6 (water-use efficiency), 7 (renewable share and clean-energy research cooperation), 8 (the Energy Transition Alliance estimate that a UK blade-recycling segment could add 20,000 jobs to offshore wind's 60,000-by-2030 target), 9, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 17. Limitations are declared inside the SDG analysis rather than buried: unknown reaction product, no demonstration of enzyme performance on real blade material, one blade type only, transport excluded by the system boundary, microplastic and BPA leaching not characterised by ReCiPe, and no penalty in the cut-off model for losing glass fibre as a resource. What happens next: the LCA inputs, assumptions and mapping code are open source, the OEM's requirements (handle multi-material blades at reasonable cost and pace) are recorded as requirements for future development rather than achievements, and relationships with State of Green, the Center for Biosolutions and DTU are described as collaborations that can continue beyond iGEM.

gemsTakeaway: Run a comparative LCA against the incumbent technologies early enough that it can still change the research plan, and publish it even when it says your own route loses - then convert each losing indicator into a named engineering target, and record the stakeholders who never replied so the gaps in your evidence base are visible rather than invisible.
